utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There's one matter before we hear the evidence of Ms. Hanson today. It's related to the bar table motion you referred to, Mr. Tieger, at the end of yesterday and also that's related to the issue which was dealt with while I was away, so I will defer to my colleague Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, it was the question of documents tendered through Dr. Treanor. There were some that were proposed to be through bar table motions, and I reminded you about the preferred method, through the witness. Now, I think that there are some outstanding documents that weren't actually dealt with, put through Mr. -- Dr. Treanor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There certainly remain documents on appendix B, which were not called up during the course of the examination-in-chief or re-direct; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Was that simply lack of time or lack of -- this isn't a criticism, that you simply forgot?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it had not -- I understood the difference -- obviously the Court's reference to its preferred method. So it was an attempt to strike a balance between the guide-lines annunciated by the Court with respect to experts that provided for the submission of documents via the bar table and attempted to do two things: Number one, identify the documents that would be most suitable to direct reference in court; and number two, not overly burden the Court with documents in the bar table submission. And they really do depend, of course, I would say, on the nature of the documents discussed and issues raised during the course of the examination-in-chief. One clear example would be where one exemplar of a particular point is made directly in examination-in-chief, and then rather than burden the Court with running through the remaining exemplars, they certainly would seem clearly to fall within the Court's guide-lines. Similarly, with respect to documents that had been contextualised and for which there would be more of a kind of pedantic or advocacy purpose served in examination-in-chief, we considered those appropriate for appendix B within the context of the Court's guide-lines. So we tried to strike a balance and not burden the Court with unnecessary time and utilise this mechanism in an appropriate way. Of course it's true that if we took additional time, which obviously in this case, as we saw yesterday, is often at a premium, all of those documents could have been addressed directly. But we understood the guide-lines to be asking the parties to strike an appropriate balance, and I believe we did so here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you got any particular position on this, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We also -- I understood basically, I think, the same way you did, that if something was important to the Prosecutor it should be presented orally through the witness. But we too, on the other hand, we run out of time and we also probably would like to take advantage of bar table motions simply because we didn't have enough time to present them. So we're constrained from disagreeing too much with Mr. Tieger because it will come back and bite us. But in any event I think we do prefer oral -- that the documents be presented orally whenever possible and would implore you to give both parties as much time as necessary for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think it's -- I'm speaking for myself, but I'm sure I speak for the Chamber, that it is the preferred method, but inevitably there's bound to be occasions when there has to be some degree of flexibility mainly because of time constraints. We don't have the luxury of unlimited time, but we can perhaps deal with this particular issue in isolation after conferring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, if I could raise one additional point, and that is we certainly have tried to invoke and use a bar table motion submission mechanism which does not simply provide the documents to the Court without illumination, but that is done in the context of a submission that identifies the relevance, where those documents fit into the case, provides an opportunity for response, and in that circumstance, I would submit, it is often the case that the Court is provided with as much contextualisation and amplification regarding that document as it would in court. I understand that the Court's interested in ensuring to the extent possible that the documents it receives are submitted in a manner that permits the Court the maximum opportunity to use them correctly, but this process has been intended to do just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you identify the items that were admitted through the course of testimony of Dr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd have to take a moment to do that, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting I would like to indicate that the Registrar has reconsidered its position concerning the prior testimony of Christian Nielson and we now withdraw our motion to obtain the prior testimony of Christian Nielson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the one which relates to Canadian court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Let's not waste court time further. [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson, given the circumstances we'll admit the -- those items that have not been dealt with through your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that those numbers will be sorted out by the Court Deputy and given number in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about only annex B, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the subject of a bar table motion. Yes. Let's call the next witness, Mr. -- Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning. The Prosecution calls Dorothea Hanson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Dorothea Curtis Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 11363, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this a copy of your curriculum vitae that you prepared in 2008?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It states there that since 1999 you've been employed by the ICTY OTP as a research officer in the leadership research team. You continued to work in the leadership research team, referred to as the LRT, as a research officer?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In addition to what's stated in the CV, you testified in 2005 as an expert in the Krajisnik case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in 2009, you testified as an expert in the Bosnian state court in the Klickovic et al. case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender the curriculum vitae of Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2588, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you were asked to prepare a report in the context of this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 23137, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document that we see on the screen, is this the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's entitled: "Expert Report, Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and War Commissions 1991 - 1995," and it's the corrected version dated the 10th of September, 2009?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please provide a brief synopsis of your experience as it relates to this report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, I was originally tasked to prepare a report -- first a memorandum on Crisis Staffs which became the expert report for the Krajisnik case. I then maintained my tasking in Crisis Staffs, regularly reviewed and updated my notes and the report, which then formed the basis of the report for the Klickovic case and also the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, and then was tasked to prepare yet a -- the most up-to-date report, this one for the Karadzic case, including a look at the War Presidencies from 1993 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you mentioned the Stanisic/Zupljanin case. You testified in that case in December 2009; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the course of preparing this report for the Karadzic case, what were the source materials that you used to write the report and draw your opinions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I looked at the contemporaneous original documents as much as I could, documents of the Bosnian Serb organs, institutions, individuals, the minutes of Crisis Staffs, decisions and conclusions of Crisis Staffs, Official Gazettes of municipalities, as well as the republic-level Official Gazettes, Assembly minutes, government minutes. I did use some contemporaneous open-source material when it seemed -- when it was relevant, when it was individuals involved in the events commenting on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And were you working with the original B/C/S documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Almost exclusively, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you read and understand B/C/S and what about Cyrillic, the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I read and understand B/C/S and Cyrillic as well as Latin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what criteria you employed when reviewing and selecting the documents that you used in your report or relied upon in your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: For my initial review, my criteria were as wide as possible, simply to find documents of the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs or about the Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and War Commissions. I did as wide a search as possible initially. And then once a pattern emerged, I would noted down those documents which best illustrated the pattern or, contrary to that, deviated significantly from the patterns that were emerging. I then noted the most relevant and the most vivid examples or articulate examples for the report itself. But behind every example there are -- can be any number of similarly relevant documents, examples -- examples which support it but not as clearly perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you assisted in identifying the documents that were potentially relevant to the topics addressed in your report by other members of the LRT; and if so, what control did you exercise over the material that was eventually relied upon in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Colleagues in the LRT and others would bring to my attention documents they found that they considered potentially relevant or if a collection had been brought in, it would be brought to my attention. But I would always review and select the documents myself. If it was one document I would look at others related to it or surrounding it, to see if they were equally relevant or, in fact, disagreed with that document. So it was always ultimately my choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in your review of documents, did you identify any documents of an exculpatory nature in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: In relation to this case or any other, when -- I did and when I did so, I would pass it on to the lawyers as part of my regular tasking to note such material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did any of those documents alter your understanding of the pattern as you have described it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No. It -- nothing made we change my mind about the pattern. I would note that there are variants especially in timing, but no, nothing -- I wouldn't have written my report as I did if I had found material that contradicted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You wished to make a few corrections to your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could please turn to paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a very embarrassing mistake and I apologise. I don't know how I omitted the word "not" from the sentence. It's very embarrassing. The first sentence of paragraph 25 should read: "Karadzic intended that the 19 December 1991 Instructions were not merely theoretical ..." I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And paragraph 83 of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here I have confused -- or I should cite to two separate minutes of government sessions, the sessions of 21 May and 23 May on the abolition of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so that paragraph should read: "The military role ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "The military role of the Crisis Staffs prior to the establishment of the Army is confirmed in the RS Government conclusions of 21 and 23 May 1992 which recommended abolishing Crisis Staffs because the army was unable to take over defence."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No, the army was taking over defence. By 21-23 May the army was taking over defence, so that's why they recommend abolishing Crisis Staffs. The conclusion of 21 May leaves a blank that is clearly meant to be abolishment but it doesn't say it. The conclusion of 23 May does specify abolishing Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, how would that paragraph read now as amended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The military role of the Crisis Staffs prior to the establishment of the army is confirmed in the RS government conclusions of 21 and 23 May which recommended abolishing Crisis Staffs as the army was taking over defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And one other small correction to paragraph 108, the first sentence should read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: "At the next Assembly session" where it currently reads "situation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's simply a wrong word. I don't know how it got there. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any objection to the report, but if I could take this opportunity to ask you what your intentions are with respect to the 34 documents that are in annex B or appendix B to this witness's notification which are also proposed for the bar table? Because I think if you don't intend to admit them, then the Prosecutor ought to know about them; and if you are thinking of admitting them, there is at least one that we have an objection to and probably they ought to be alerted to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note those documents are so-called source documents, aren't they, Ms. Sutherland, cited in the -- in an expert's report?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour. But we would be seeking to have the documents admitted for the truth of the contents as well as a source document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So has it not been our practice that with respect to those source documents, unless they are dealt with during the course of the expert's testimony, we do not admit it as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Trial Chamber has previously admitted source documents tendered in the same manner as the documents in appendix B and noted that this method of tendering documents was consistent with the guide-lines and previous decisions. And that was in relation to the expert witness Dr. Donia, and that's trial transcript 1st of June, 2010, at pages 3151, line 19, to 3152, line 8. And can I add that the Prosecution has been selective in the appendix B documents and concentrated on what is at issue between the parties as far as we're able to anticipate it. The documents are placed into context in the reports and will be further contextualised by Ms. Hanson during her testimony this morning. In addition, the Prosecutor has satisfied the other requirements for the admission of the documents from the bar table generally and that's pursuant to your order on the procedure for the conduct of the trial of the 8th of October, 2009, appendix A, part 7, paragraph R. And for these reasons, the Prosecution would ask at the end of Ms. Hanson's testimony that appendix B documents be admitted in connection with the report and for all other purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond to this submission, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Our preference would be that any comments on these documents be elicited orally from the witness, and we think it burdens the whole record and it especially burdens us given the limitations on us we're given when documents are admitted from the bar table. On the other hand, we realise that if there is going to be bar table motions, then this is probably -- most of them come within what could maybe be filed as a bar table motion near the end of the case or at some point during the case. And on balance we prefer that as much of the information that the Chamber receives be received orally but that we also be given enough time to present our side of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I can say about this is the following three. First, the bar table motion, as we indicated earlier on, should be the last resort. Second, we would -- the Chamber would encourage you to deal with documents as much as possible with the witness through the course of your examination. Third, if there are remaining documents which are not dealt with with the witness, we will issue an informed decision so that this issue will not arise again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just ask Mr. Robinson if he could advise the document in appendix B that they would be objecting to so that I can decide whether I wish to deal with it in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. That's item number 22 which is a newspaper article, which you've consistently held are not admissible through bar table motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I would now like to turn to the origins of the Crisis Staffs. You will see two binders down beside the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are documents that are cited in appendix A and appendix B. I have shown them to Mr. Robinson prior to placing them near the table at -- will assist Ms. Hanson if she has hard copies in front of her while the documents are being brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, were the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs operating from late 1991 an entirely new phenomenon or did they have some kind of legal precedent?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: In the legislature of the SFRY and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia as well as some municipal statutes that I've been able to examine, there were provisions for a collective body to operate in the municipalities in times of war or other emergencies. There were also provisions for the committees or councils for All People's Defence which were seen as emergency bodies in case of war, invasion, for the municipal authorities and police and military and party to run -- to be the municipal authorities until such time as government was re-established. So yes, there were some origins, but I've never seen the term "Crisis Staff" itself in any of these -- any of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain for the Court when and how the SDS Crisis Staffs came to be formed.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They were formed on the basis of the instructions issued by the SDS Main Board dated 19 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Under the instructions what was the role of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: To first prepare for the creation of Serb municipal -- Serb Municipal Assemblies, Serbian municipal forces, organs; and then to actually be the municipal governments of the new Serbian municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are currently two versions of Variant A and B instructions in evidence, P0005 and P00960. I would like to show P00960, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is referred to in paragraph 20 in footnote 17 of your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, I think we forgot to give the number to her report. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2589.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was this the instruction that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is number 93. There are several versions in the possession of the OTP with different numbers. This is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many municipalities were there in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I believe 107 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the highest number of the copies found in the OTP's collections?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I think 104 or -- I'd have to check my notes, but it's not more than 107.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What inference, if any, do you draw from that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to pause between question and answer in order for everything that you are saying to be interpreted correctly and so that the transcript can be complete.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that different numbers have been found in different municipalities, I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Hanson. I'm sorry to interrupt you. Your question was not reflected fully. Could you repeat your question, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that the highest number of the copies found in OTP's collection was 104, numbered 104. What inference, if any, do you draw from that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Given that different numbers of this document were found in different municipalities and the highest number is close to the number of municipalities, I infer that each municipality received one copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English and also page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Item 4 states: "In order to ensure their consistent and timely implementation, tasks, measures and other activities shall be set forth in two variants, A and B, and at two levels." Can you just remind the Court what Variant A and B refer to.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Variant A are the majority -- municipalities where the Serbs were majority of the population. Variant B was Serb minority municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what are the two levels referred to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The first degree and the second degree, "stepen."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the first level aimed at?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The first level was aimed at preparations for creating Serb municipalities, creating a Crisis Staff as a shadow government, including the various Serb office-holders in the municipality and people with links to the party centre, such as Main Board members and deputies, calling a Serb Assembly, making all the preparations also as far as TO, police, and commodity reserves. The second degree was the actual take-over of police stations and the putting into action of the municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do these instructions make any explicit reference to the establishment of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they call for the formation of Crisis Staffs in both Variant A and Variant B first level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think we can see that in item 3?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it lists the people who should be in the Crisis Staff, the leaders of the SDS municipal board, Serbs holding office in the municipality, or the SDS candidates for those positions, deputies to the Assembly, members of the Main Board, chief of police, commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In footnote 17 of your report -- do you have a copy of your report in front of you? It's in -- is it in the front of the binder?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In footnote 17 of your report you list eight copies of the instructions.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, from Gorazde, Livno, Trnovo, Bosanski Petrovac, and the others found in various locations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to now move on from the actual instructions to look at the municipal boards acting upon them. What did your examination of the material show with regard to how this instruction was distributed and to whom it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The evidence I have been able to examine indicates that the instructions were distributed at an expanded meeting of the SDS, that is, the Main Board and municipal board presidents or Municipal Assembly presidents, on the 20th of December. Some may have been distributed the next day at an Assembly -- Bosnian Serb Assembly session. They were distributed to the municipalities and received and implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could look briefly at some examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 08117 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is entitled: "Conclusions of SDS Zvornik municipal board meeting held on the 22nd of December, 1991." Do you see any relationship between this document and the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. Two days after the instructions were distributed, the SDS municipal board in Zvornik is taking steps consistent with the 19 December instructions, the duty service, the Crisis Staff in a make-up that is consistent with the A and B instructions. For example, the commander of the Crisis Staff is Branko Grujic, the president of the SDS municipal board. The next member listed, Jovo Mijatovic, is the deputy to the Bosnian Serb Assembly from Zvornik. The -- it mentions a co-ordinator for negotiations with the SDA, that's also in the 19 December instructions. So it's consistent with it, and we've seen other documents in Zvornik that explicitly refer to the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there's another document on appendix B, 65 ter 11239, the declaration of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, and that directly cites Article 4 of the instructions for the organisation of the operations of the Serbian people in the municipalities of 19 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 08117 will be Exhibit P2590.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to have that admitted also. I wasn't going to call it up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 11239 will be Exhibit P2591.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A second example is from the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 00979.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the 6th meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS municipal board of Kljuc dated the 23rd of December, 1991. Looking in particular at the preamble, is there anything of significance here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: By "preamble," do you mean the agenda? The briefing on the decisions of the Serbian Assembly and the materials that arrived, and then under that agenda item it says that: "Veljko Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in BH. All the organs will be required to act in accordance with these instructions." I take that to be a reference to the 19 December instructions amongst other things because it then lists the member of the -- forms a Crisis Staff, lists the members, and other tasks consistent with the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what does Brane Vojvodic have to say about the matter?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: He says: "I can accept all Karadzic's proposals without seeing them." In fact, later in the same meeting, they say -- Kondic says: You don't need yet to know what the second degree is because it's just -- the first degree is preparation for the second. So it's another reference to, You don't need to know everything but if Karadzic is sending it, we're going to do it, it seems to say. I would also note that the Assembly deputy is there and briefing the municipal board on the activities of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The third example is from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 08176, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the minutes of the SDS Crisis Staff for Sarajevo dated the 24th of December, 1991. And what is the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Again, it's a reference to implementing the 19 December instructions because, as you see towards the bottom of the page, it said: "Particular tasks as per the instructions on the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in BH in emergency situations according to Variant 'B' under first degree ..." Then it lists a number of items. It says, for example, number 7, well, paragraph 7 of B first degree refers to information and propaganda activities and there a member of SDS information council is assigned a task. Number 8 in Variant B first degree refers to police and TO. Mico Stanisic is in the Bosnian police, so it's entirely consistent. The make-up is consistent. The first name listed, Jovo Jovanovic, is a member of the SDS Main Board and SDS Executive Board. It appears to be an implementation of the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is in evidence as Exhibit P2532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The fourth example is from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I could have P00975, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Ilidza proclaiming the foundation of the Assembly of Serbian municipality of Ilidza number 6 of 92. Looking in particular at the preamble, is there anything of significance here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. They reference the instructions, with the instructions of the Serbian Democratic Party Main Board number 79. I haven't seen any copy with 79 on it, but that system of referring to it is consistent with the front page as we've seen with the 19 December instructions. Proclaiming a Serbian Assembly is one of the -- is part of the instructions. I've seen several such declarations that cite the main -- that cite the 19 December instructions in their preamble. I would also draw your attention to paragraph 5 which says that the Assembly will recognise federal regulations and those municipal regulations which are not contrary to federal regulations and the interests of the Serbian people. So this is a specific declaration that the Serbian Municipal Assembly will follow only those laws that it feels are in the interest of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in the English and the B/C/S and the distribution list?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it shows that it was forwarded to the President of the Serbian Assembly, that is Momcilo Krajisnik, and the president of the SDS BH, Radovan -- that would be Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour. Sorry, it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, to understand the difficulty of my colleague Judge Lattanzi, I was hearing through French but if you could -- if you could put a pause in between the question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I apologise to Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The last example is from the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 11239.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a decision regarding the formation of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the wrong page is highlighted in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Go to page 2 in the English and page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Item 3 --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Item --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's the significance of this item?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Item 3 says that the Serb -- certain parts of the municipality of Zvornik, including parts of the town, are being separated from the existing municipality of Zvornik and becoming part of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. I would also note that once again the preamble cites Article 4 of the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on page 4 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, under item 9 of -- it states that the declaration is to be published in "Javnost." What do you infer from this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: "Javnost" was the newspaper of the SDS so that I infer that this was knowledge within at least the SDS or the Serbian part of -- the Serbs of Bosnia. I would also note that I've seen identical decisions from at least three other municipalities, Tuzla, Donji Vakuf, and Kalesija. They used the exact same wording with the only differences being obviously the names of the communities entering and the number of Assembly members.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document you just referred to in relation to Tuzla is on appendix B and that's 65 ter 11498. And the one related to Donji Vakuf is also listed and that's 65 ter 00499.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see those two documents, Mr. Robinson, 11498 and 499?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't think it's necessary. But I would just like to point out -- it's not an objection but I would point out that these are two municipalities that are not included in the indictment, but I understand that for contextual reasons it's relevant, but I would just point that out for its weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, I seek to tender the Zvornik document, which is 11239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has already been admitted. You dealt with it a minute ago. Exhibit P2591. And we'll admit the other two, 11498 and 499.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2593 and P2594, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, without bringing the document up, it's 65 ter 00982, it's in relation to the Prijedor municipality of the 27th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's another -- further evidence of the receipt and implementation of A and B. I see several SDS municipal board minutes, information on Variant A and B being discussed, and Prijedor is another example of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document, that's also listed on appendix B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as P2595.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I now wish to turn to discuss the importance of Variant A and B. What importance did Mr. Karadzic place on the instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: He considered the instructions vitally important for the creation of municipal governments and the take-over of real functions, as he described it. He made several references, both at the time and in later years, to the importance of A and B -- I'm sorry, 19 December instructions. They are often known informally as Variant A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 30537, and in particular, page 7 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is an intercepted telephone conversation between a person named Miroslav and Radovan Karadzic held on the 7th of January, 1992. Did you listen to the audio of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. For all the intercepts cited in my report I listened to the audio, if available. I listened to many other intercepts as well, but I just want to reassure the Court I've listened to the audio. And here Karadzic is discussing who should be in charge in the ARK, and he says he doesn't want some scientist from the academy. It's -- not a university professor because it's not a time for science. It is a time to take over real functions -- as it is in the B/C/S, it's -- with many intercepts it's a lot of ellipses, but he says: This, this, this, that, that, that, real functions in the sense of that paper of ours, level 1, level 2. So he's being clear that it's not just theory, it's time to take real action and really make our governments function, and A and B will be a guidance for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to have marked for identification the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2596, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did Mr. Karadzic make any speeches in the -- you said that Mr. Karadzic spoke in later years. Was that at the Assembly sessions in relation to the instructions or Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994 and in 1995 he referred to how A and B had given them guide-lines at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could quickly call up 65 -- sorry, P01403. This is the Assembly session of the 11th of November, 1994. If we could go to page 347 of the English and e-court page 304 of the B/C/S. It's ERN 0215-3546.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can see in the English that Mr. Karadzic begins to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then if we can go to page 348 of the English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just note, if I'm allowed, that the English translation as provided is not correct in one sentence. Could I read the B/C/S? The first -- he says: [Interpretation] "Everything's clear as day to us in municipalities ..." [In English] The English translation for some reason has not -- not everything. The B/C/S is: "Everything was clear to us." He is saying: "Everything is clear to us. We had instruct -- do you remember instruction A and instruction B? We had Crisis Staffs and it was clear that they were the authority. They could make mistakes but they were the authority. People were not left without authority because there was a Crisis Staff." So he explicitly refers to A and B, that is the 19 December instructions, as creating Crisis Staffs and creating Serbian authority in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 60 -- sorry, P00970, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the transcript from the 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly held on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 144 of the English and 175 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is set out in paragraph 27 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see the reference in the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- page 145.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I am familiar with this quotation, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the English translation is not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Actually, it's -- the quote of Mr. Karadzic is set out in paragraph 27 of your report --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better to go to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So if you could just explain the significance of the quote.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is during an Assembly that was discussing the army in somewhat heated terms and Karadzic is tying the A and B instructions not only to municipal governments but also to the army. "At the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, municipal boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B variants."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see it from this exhibit? Where can we locate it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's on page 144 to 145 of the English and 175 and 176 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The translation -- the ERN which is cited in the report is actually from a different translation, but we simply used the exhibit that was already admitted in court so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: If another page of the B/C/S could be brought out, it's at 00846058. I don't know if that's possible here. Oh, no, it's only one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is that possible, to bring up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It would be going forward about 53 pages in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'll read the B/C/S and you can listen to the translation. [Interpretation] "At the moment when the war began we -- everything was perfectly clear to us that those municipalities -- in the municipalities where we were the minority we set up secret governments, municipal boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B variants."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, still we haven't found the English page number. So that's the problem with the -- admitting without seeing the document. We have to spend days to locate this passage outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have my copy marked, but I don't see the sticker now. Uh-huh, it's -- it's on -- at the bottom of the English it's on page 347 of 350 in the footnote. Mr. Registrar, do you see just at the bottom here 347 of 350?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, but the document we are seeing is of 376 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah -- no, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm at the wrong exhibit. I do apologise for that. It's on page 145 of 376, which is the original page number I took you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are on that page in e-court, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, we can return to it after the break if necessary. I can locate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. In the meantime, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hanson, in paragraph 26 of your report you state that municipal leaders consulted with the SDS leadership on how to implement the instructions. I wasn't going to bring the document up, but do you recall any reference made in an Assembly session in 1993 regarding Mr. Karadzic's involvement in the issuance of the instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993, the Jajce municipal president refers to consultations he had the previous year with Karadzic and Krajisnik on how to implement A and B. He makes it very clear that it was A and B, and "in accordance with the order issued by Mr. Karadzic, I asked Mr. Karadzic at a counselling what I was to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is referred to in footnote 27 of the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- there's -- I also refer to an intercept in which the -- some -- someone from the Sarajevo Centar municipal board calls Karadzic on the 1st of January, 1992, and says: We've got the instructions but we need some help in implementing them. So I take that as another request for help in implementing A and B, although it does -- not as explicit as saying Variant A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After Variant A and B document was issued in -- at the end of December or on the -- around the 20th of December, 1991, was reference made in front of Karadzic in any Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. Jovan Cizmovic at the session in late January 1992 called for what he termed an urgent operationalisation of the Serbian Republic, that is, I take it to mean actually putting all the government organs into operation; tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out. So it's an explicit reference to the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's P01349, the transcript from the 6th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly on the 26th of January, 1992. I don't intend on calling that document up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we are on wrong number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, actually I will call it up for Your Honour. It's P01349. The problem the -- the document that we had the problem with, Your Honour, was the 50th Session of the Assembly in 1995. I'm going now back to immediately after the instructions were issued to the Assembly session in early January -- late January 1992. So if we can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Cizmovic's quote is on page 14 of the English, and the B/C/S ERN is -- at e-court page 29 and the ERN is SA02-5260.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you see the quote that you -- the reference that you made a moment ago, do you see that on the pages that are on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, the second-to-last paragraph, "starting to solve this problem ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, did anything further happen relating to Variant A and B within two to three weeks of this session?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of February at a session of -- expanded session, I believe municipal presidents and so on, Karadzic called for the implementation of the second degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 01000 -- sorry, and this is P0012. English page 17 and 24 -- that we'd go to page 17 and the B/C/S page 18, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does Karadzic say there that the stage number 2 should also be converted, "the one we've talked about, the one you have, if not here, then at home. In order to -- in order to have authorities in the field functioning"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's at line -- around line 16 --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: 16, 17 it starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does he then say there: "That is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level, and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's another reference to the second level. In the B/C/S it's "stepen," which is also translated as "degree," it's the same word. He also earlier in his speech makes other references to the second degree, including one where he says: "You know that paper of mine, that paper," and the audience responds "we know," which I take to be another acknowledgement of the receipt and just knowledge of A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to an example of the implementation of the activation of this second degree in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 00594 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's an extract from the minutes of the meeting of the Bratunac Serbian SDS municipal board on the 24th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's page 20 in the English. Yes, the chairman of the SDS municipal board Miroslav Deronjic is briefing the Bratunac board on introduction on the -- information on the second degree of the state of emergency. Deronjic read the material about the second degree which he received from the central office and said that: "It was an order which we are obliged to carry out." The English is a little more confused than the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And another related document that you have on appendix B is actually the first document on appendix B, the 65 ter 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, let us find the passage Ms. Hanson referred to. We are all on page 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Given that the first degree of the state of emergency alert was declared and it lasted until today, therefore the second degree of the state of emergency is to be declared as of now. Deronjic read the material about the second degree which he received from the central office ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, Ms. Hanson, another document that's related to the Bratunac municipality is the first document on appendix B, 65 ter 00595, which is an extract from the minutes of the meeting of the Bratunac SDS municipal board of the 23rd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's also indication that they received A and B. It's -- it specifies there there are two variants, A and B, which he received, he said, from the Presidency of the SDS Sarajevo. So from the leadership of the SDS he received A and B. There is also reference to the activation of the second degree in Prijedor minutes from about this time, second half of February. And I believe --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was the exhibit -- sorry, that's been exhibited as P2595, the Prijedor document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I seek to tender the Bratunac document that's listed on appendix B, 00595.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, would you like to see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2598, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I don't know what time we're rising for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 10.30, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I now want to move on to the section in your report, which is starting at page 15, entitled: "From Party Organ to Municipal Government, January to April 1992." You describe the evolution or change in the character of the Crisis Staffs from -- in that period, but can you briefly tell the Court what happened between the 14th of February until the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This is at the time when at the republic level the Bosnian Serb Assembly is passing constitution and other laws which transform the -- which establish the Bosnian Serb state and transform their party organs into the government organs of the Bosnian Serb state. And we see the same thing at the municipal level. The 19 December instructions were the guide-lines to set it up -- set up the Crisis Staff, set up the municipal government, and the emphasis especially in March 1992 is now to make those changes real on the ground, establish the ethnic separation on the ground, as Krajisnik refers to it. And we see the Assembly deputies asking for instructions in the Assembly. The connection -- while the Crisis Staffs were simply party organs, the connection is through the Assembly because Assembly deputies were members of the municipal Crisis Staffs. So we see people like Vjestica from Bosanska Krupa reporting in the Assembly on what they've accomplished in establishing Serbian authority in the municipalities, asking for instructions. So we see by April 1992 that the Crisis Staffs themselves transform from SDS party organs to publicly declaring themselves the municipal authorities in the Serbian municipalities. So it's a move from party to public government functions that parallels what the Assembly is doing at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you mentioned that in March 1992 that the members and the deputies were seeking instruction in the Assembly. Was -- without calling the documents up, was Mr. Karadzic providing any instruction in March Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, he says you will get instructions but not in the Assembly, in the Deputies Club. I would note that the Assembly transcripts -- had official transcripts. We don't have transcripts of the Deputies Club meetings, but it's almost exactly the same make-up, it's just that -- the same people there just calling themselves the Deputies Club rather than the Assembly. But he assures them that they will get instructions. Branko Djeric, the prime minister, also assures them that they will get instructions and that it will all be done together by a secret signal to take-over the municipalities. I believe he says "secret."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is dealt with in paragraphs 33 and 34 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "We can form whatever we want. The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. At a given moment in the next three or four days, there will be a single method and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, both things that must be done as well as how to do them, how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command. I think we shall hear it today in the form of instructions at the Deputies Club." And he goes on at the next session of the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, that was the 24th of March, 1992, Assembly session, the 12th Session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's Exhibit P00961 for Your Honours' and Mr. Karadzic's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then he goes on?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: At the 27th of March, he is telling the Assembly deputies to go sit next to the municipal presidents and carry out our policies. So we can see the deputies as the channel for republic-level policy to be implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when was the move of Crisis Staffs from party to governmental organ completed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, I see a significant step in that. On the 4th of April, 1992, when Karadzic issues an announcement which says Crisis Staffs should be activated and he is issuing it not as president of the SDS but as president of the National Security Council, a government position rather than a party position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 0587 -- oh, no, Exhibit D00394 on the screen, please. And, Your Honour, while that's coming up, the 27 March 1992 Assembly session is 65 ter 00023 and I don't just have at the moment the exhibit number, but that was already -- that has been exhibited in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen now, Exhibit D00394, what is the significance of the public announcement?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, the letter-head says it comes from the Assembly of the Serbian People, the Council for National Defence, so government organs. Karadzic signs it as president of the council, and in the last paragraph he says that Crisis Staffs should be activated in those places where -- he's telling them not to -- not to obey the Rump BH Presidency, as he refers to the government -- the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia. And he tells them that in those areas where people are obeying the Bosnian Presidency, Crisis Staffs should be activated, and Serbian people's TO, civilian protection, and reserve police raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hanson, just before the break we dealt with the document from Sanski Most dated the 16th of April, 1992. Going on from there, as the Crisis Staffs came out into the open, did they receive any direction from the republican government as to how they should operate?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did. On the 26th of April, the president of the government, Branko Djeric, issued the instructions for the work of the Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit D00407 on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is an extract from the instructions for the work of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian nation in the municipalities. This is the document you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you through a few of the instructions, and this is dealt with in paragraphs 39 to 41 of your report. Item 1, which is on page 1 on the -- both English and B/C/S, can you just explain the authority there.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This states clearly that: "... the Crisis Staff takes over all the prerogatives and functions of the Municipal Assemblies when they are unable to convene." So the Crisis Staff is becoming the highest authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to item 2, again on the same page, it sets out the composition of the Crisis Staffs. Is this consistent with the composition set out in the 19 December 1991 instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's consistent. It brings together the TO, the police, other forces or organisations necessary and to -- the most important resources and forces in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With respect to item 3?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Its job is to co-ordinate all these municipal organs to defend the territory, maintain security, establish authority, organise day-to-day life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And does that set out the Crisis Staff's role in relation to military affairs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Not -- not explicitly by itself, but it certainly says that the Crisis Staff's most important job is defence and security and authority, so it does not specify -- later on it -- yes, the next one, Article 4, specifies that the Crisis Staff is to prevent other people interfering with the command of the TO or police forces. They are a professional staff, let them do their job, but the Crisis Staff co-ordinates the overall activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And item 6, is that outlining the Crisis Staff's -- what their actions shall be based upon?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. Item 6 clearly places the Crisis Staff in the Bosnian Serb state system, saying that they are to work in accordance with the constitution and law as well as decisions brought by the Assembly, the Presidency, and the Government of the Bosnian Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you have any comment in relation to item 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could scroll down the page -- the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is 26 April, when it was still the JNA was the armed -- was still in Bosnia, and it shows the -- they are to support the JNA and -- support it and take-over its property -- well, assume its position, but as we know, in practice that was taking over army property after having consulted with the government level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can go to page -- sorry, item 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you have any comment in relation to that item?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's interesting that they -- it says that to the non-combatant people, the Crisis Staff should act in accordance with the International Red Cross, towards POWs act according to the laws of the Serbian Republic. But, clearly both of those categories of people are considered to be the business of the Crisis Staff, prisoners of war and non-combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And paragraph 11 talks about a duty to report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Item 11, sorry.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, the duty of the Crisis Staff to gather information, inform and consult the proper organs of the Serbian Republic, that is, government representatives -- yes, the word here is translated as "representatives," but it's an important word that we'll see a lot in the future. So I would note that in the B/C/S it's "povjerenik," which is usually translated as "commissioner" because this is a person whose job is to be their contact person -- be the Crisis Staff's contact person at the republic level, the personal link between -- we'll see more about him -- about the "povjerenik" later. But it shows that Crisis Staffs again are part of the state system, obliged to inform and consult. We see this also in item 14 where they are supposed to submit weekly reports to regional and state organs. So they're part of the state system receiving policy and instructions and reporting back on their implementation by the "povjerenik" as a go-between. I also would note in item 14 that the Crisis Staff is to work collectively, bring decisions in full complement means with all the people present, which is another important aspect of how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I now want to turn to Crisis Staffs receiving and acting upon instructions, and this is -- starts at paragraph 43 of your report. Acting upon the 26th April instructions.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, we see evidence in many municipalities that these instructions were received and acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 05724.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters again kindly note for a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On your review of this document, to what extent, if at all, does the wording of this document reflect the 26 April 1992 instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Some articles are almost a literal transcription of the 26 April instructions and lead me to believe that they received the instructions and implemented them at their level. For example, Article 2 is the same as Article 3 of the 26 April instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Article 4?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Article 4 is consistent with the composition as instructed in the 26 April instructions. Article 11 of the Prijedor instruction is a paraphrasing of almost exact wording, except for using -- inserting Prijedor, as the last Article, Article 14, of the 26 April instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there they regard the Crisis Staff as intermediaries; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they include them as another -- another organ. In fact, Article 12 makes clear that it is intermediary level because they shall consult first the ARK and then the republic level if necessary and feasible. So the ARK is their first level, the republic level is the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in regard to Article 9, this is on page 4 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S, "maintaining co-operation via senior officers of these institutions," what does this indicate with regard to the lines of command of the police and other bodies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The senior officers of the JNA units, the TO, civilian defence, and police were part of the Crisis Staffs. So the Crisis Staff creates the co-operation of these units by bringing the senior officers together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you also see these instructions being -- the 26 April 1992 instructions being followed in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. I note several in my footnote where I see reference to it or quotations from. I also see a document from the Executive Board of the SDS itself, saying that these instructions have been forwarded and are valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, in your report you talk about War Presidencies and War Commissions. This is at paragraphs 45 to 55. Can you explain what the difference was between the Crisis Staffs and the War Presidencies and War Commissions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I use "Crisis Staff" as an umbrella term for all three when talking about the actions of these bodies because they were seen as very much the same body in the ground -- on the ground and in practice. The War Presidencies were established according to a decision of the Bosnian Serb Presidency of 31 May 1992, and it says that with that decision, Crisis Staffs ceased to operate; however, the terms are used interchangeably. All the bodies emphasised the continuity between and their tasks are the same. So I see them as simply the next stage in the development of Crisis Staffs because the Bosnian Serb state is now writing its laws, setting up its institutions, so rather than being -- Crisis Staffs being formed by the SDS Main Board instructions of December 1991, this is a decision of the Presidency giving -- making their reporting lines and their whole basis through the state organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can look at three documents in relation to War Presidencies and war commissions, the first document is 05966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does your -- Ms. Hanson, does your previous answer also relate to War Commissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- that decision and the formation of commissions are a little more problematical, but certainly I use -- when I say "Crisis Staffs" and I talk about their operations, I am also including War Commissions as they operated as the municipal -- the highest municipal authority. When we look at the decision on War Commissions, I'll explain the differ -- the way in which they differ, but in practice they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that you use "Crisis Staff" as an umbrella term for all three when talking about the actions of these bodies. And was that because the terminology was used interchangeably by the actual authorities on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. We often see them meeting in the same -- the same composition and saying, "Oh, today we're a War Presidency, we're no longer a Crisis Staff." We see them saying that the name will be changed formally but what we are actually doing remains the same. This decision on the formation of War Presidencies gives them the same tasking. Clearly they are the same body, but simply now being formalised as a state body, that is, being made part of the legislature. And I think the term "War Presidency" is a more formal term. As we see, there was legislative precedent for a collective Presidency and nowhere in the previous legislation do we see the term "Crisis Staff," and that is a more informal sounding term, but to call it a War Presidency makes it clear that it is the municipal Presidency and its tasks, as we see in Article 3, are very much the same as the Crisis Staff taskings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're looking now at document 05966 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, the War Presidency shall organise, co-ordinate, and adjust activities for the defence of the Serbian people, create and ensure conditions for the work of military organs and units defending the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is dated the 31st of May, 1992, and it was in the Official Gazette which was published on the 8th of June, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 18328.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's a memo by Trifko Komad, SDS BH Executive Board secretary, re the formation of War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned this document before. In the first paragraph he refers to the 26 April instructions, you'll note, and now he's saying, "Those that you've already received for Crisis Staffs, well, now we're forming War Presidencies." And just to note the confusion of terms, within one paragraph he refers to the decision on Presidencies but then he says, "Instead of Crisis Staffs War Commissions are being formed." The translation -- the English translation is not correct. These terms are tricky but I will read it. It says: [No interpretation]. [In English] Commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read it again. It has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How should it read in English in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commissions. [Interpretation] War commissions, war time commissions. [In English] Yes, war commissions. I just note that that indicates the confusion even at the republican level of these terms because all of these bodies had the person of the commissioner, "povjerenik," who, as I said, is the link -- the path for communications. But this is significant because it's the SDS Executive Board telling the presidents of regional Crisis Staffs that they should now implement this decision on the formation of War Presidencies, and if they have any further questions, contact the republic Presidency directly, which shows again how the party organs are now becoming state organs. The state is taking over from the party. The party is forwarding these instructions to government -- people in a position of government presumably and telling them: If you have any more questions, talk to the Presidency about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- I think the report is 2582, the expert report.
