utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Very well. We have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's at footnote 55 we have Bihac and then 65 ter number in bold at the end of the decision, and then Bosanska Dubica the same, 65 ter 17202. And then if we go over the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I confirmed it. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- and we can see all these 65 ter numbers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Do you have any objections to the admission of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 17223 will be Exhibit P2609, and 65 ter 17202 will be Exhibit P2610.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then on the page we're now looking at, Bosanska Gradiska is 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's all of the -- there's Gradiska, Novi Petrovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have the third document in relation to the War Presidencies and War Commissions on the screen and that is 65 ter 05917. And this is the decision on the formation of War Commissions in municipalities in time of war or imminent threat of war dated the 10th of June, 1992, which was published in the Official Gazette on the 30th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you explain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This document is similar to the 31st of May decision that we saw on the formation of War Presidencies. It makes no reference to that decision, so I do find some difficulty in saying how these two relate to each other. But it clearly says that War Commissions as constituted will take-over from Crisis Staffs, they will supersede Crisis Staffs. So it's the same intention. Article 3 on their work is very similar to the wording of the War Presidency. "The War Commissions shall maintain the closest possible co-operation with the legal authorities; they shall convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the republic; they shall convey information about the problems, needs, and work of the municipal bodies via their commissioners; they shall co-operate with the authorities with a view to creating conditions for the work of military organs and units engaged in defending the Serbian people." The difference -- the most significant difference I find between these two decisions is the amount of text emphasising the work of the commissioner himself. It makes it clear that he has the authority to dissolve the War Commissions and appoint new members in consultation with the republic Presidency. Could I see some more article -- the next pages -- is there more or not? Oh, no, it does refer -- I'm sorry, the text. It does -- it says it -- I didn't see the -- before, that it does say it takes -- it supersedes the decision on War Presidencies, but in fact we don't see War Commissions established everywhere and we see War Presidencies operating in June and July a lot more than we see War Commissions. As I understand the distinction -- well, the -- the make -- the composition as described in this decision is a much smaller body than the War Presidency, and it seems to be intended for those places where the municipal authorities were functioning the worst, where there was more need for an outsider to come and make sure everything could function. We first see War Commissions established pursuant to this decision in Eastern Bosnia, the area known as Birac. I don't see them, for example, in the ARK, so they're not everywhere; whereas we do see War Presidencies and even Crisis Staffs operating in June and July everywhere. Where I do have documents of a War Commission, they are operating just the same as a War Presidency in a larger composition than this decision says. So I think although this decision looks like it's a somewhat different body that's supposed to replace both Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, in practice where War Commissions functioned they acted much the same as Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies. And I don't see many documents of War Commissions operating as this instruction -- as this decision would lay out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you said, the Crisis Staffs continued to operate, and did they continue to receive instructions from the republic level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. They received orders from the republic level. They reported to the republic level. They were still seen as a body. It was seen simply as a difference in terminology in practice. In Rajlovac, for example, the president of the municipality said: First we had a Crisis Staff, then a War Presidency, then a War Commission, then a War Presidency again. In practice the terms were much the same. We see the confusion of terms noted even by the -- at the government level saying, People aren't satisfied with these terms. So it's taken -- it seems to be different terms are used for essentially one and the same body. I certainly never see a Crisis Staff and a War Commission operating in the same place at the same time. It's one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we'll take a look at a few examples of Crisis Staffs receiving orders and implementing policies from the republic level shortly, but before that just talking about the role of the Crisis Staffs in the Bosnian Serb state, which you deal with at paragraphs 56 to 65 of your report, once they were fully established in April 1992, what was the level of authority at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs declared themselves to be the highest municipal authority with all the rights and functions and authority of the Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in a nutshell what was their main role?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: To co-ordinate all the forces and resources of the municipality to establish Serbian power on the ground and to be the municipal government of the Serbian municipalities. They brought together the party, the government, the military, the police, and any other resources as needed to make sure that their actions on the ground were co-ordinated with the highest level of policy and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said that they received this direction. From which organs, which bodies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They implemented decisions of the Presidency, the government, the -- one of their taskings was also to carry out the policies of the Main Staff of the VRS. We see them acknowledging all of those organs as their authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you have two examples in appendix B, 65 ter 017 -- no, sorry. 65 ter 17217, which is the government session held on the 21st of May, which is referred to in paragraph 60 of your report; and 65 ter 05057, which is the Sanski Most document dated the 22nd of May, 1992, which referred to Mr. Karadzic and the government session held on the 21st of May, 1992, re the issue of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. When the Presidency issued a decree on mobilisation -- a declaration on mobilisation, the government then passed it on to all levels, including all municipal Crisis Staffs. And we see Sanski Most implementing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, without calling those two documents up, I would seek to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They will be admitted

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 05917 will be Exhibit P2611; 65 ter 17217 will be Exhibit P2612; and 65 ter 05057 will be Exhibit P2613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I now want to take you to look at one regional level document and three municipal level documents in relation to the Crisis Staffs and the recognition of the authority of the RS government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter 04835, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most reached at a meeting on the 30th of May, 1992. Can you explain the significance of this document in relation to the recognition of the authority of the government?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Under item 1 it says: "Nedeljko Rasula, the president of the Crisis Staff, co-ordinates and harmonises the work of our Crisis Staff for the Crisis Staff of ARK," which shows the co-ordination with the regional level. The next item, 2, says that: "Vlado Vrkes, the deputy president, is in charge of political problems and the implementation of the ideas of the Serbian Democratic Party leadership at the level of the republic, region, and municipality." We also see that there's a -- the other forces are mentioned, TO, police, and so on, but the second right up there is the idea of co-ordinating with the region and implementing the party ideas at the level of republic, region, and municipality. So it's a recognition of the authority. And later on under -- towards the bottom of the page we see them saying that they want to get in touch with the ARK leadership regarding implementation of the idea on resettlement of the population. So they're consulting with the regional level on how to implement on the ground in this case resettlement of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does it appear to you -- from what I understand with the republic, regional, and municipal level that it's -- the removal of the non-Serb population, what sort of effort is that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's co-ordinated, as we see from many documents that I cite. It's considered policy and it's co-ordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next document is 65 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the Serbian page 2, please. Well, actually page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 11502 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's the decision by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Autonomous Region Birac dated the 29th of April, 1992. What is the basis and the significance of this decision?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This decision shows the republic -- the regional level acting on a republic-level decision, implementing it and passing it on and using that to -- passing it on to the municipal level and using that to grant authority to the municipal level. It says: "Pursuant to the Decision of the Council for National Security of the Serbian Republic of BH on general mobilisation ... the Crisis Staff of SAO Birac proclaims a state of war ... in the territory of entire autonomous region." And if we can have the next page it says that: "... mobilisation shall be carried out by municipal staffs ..." So here we see the republic-level decision passed on by the regional to the municipal to implement, and it says: "All units, including the existing military ones, shall come under the command of the municipal Crisis Staffs and the Crisis Staff of SAO Birac." At the last part indicates their role in the state. Again, they're subject to the legal sanctions in force in the Serbian Republic. So this is very much part of the Serbian state system and it uses a republic-level decision to say that the municipal Crisis Staffs are now commanding all military units in the area, which we'll see later in the military section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2615, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the document referred to -- the republic-level document referred to in this decision we will be going to in a moment, that's 65 ter 00153. If the next document that could be brought up on the screen is 65 ter 01064. This is a proposal number 184/92 from the War Presidency of Bosanska Krupa to the command of the 1st Krajina Podgrmec Brigade on the 25th of May, 1992, signed by Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, what's the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: There's a lot to be seen from it, but I would quickly note this is an example of a pre-31 May War Presidency. So the term was being used. But most importantly here, it's the War Presidency proposing an action to the local brigade basing its reason on, number 1, as we see under reasons, the decision -- the political determination to have the border of the Serbian entity be along the river Una. On the 16th of May -- sorry, the 12th of May, the 16th Assembly Session, the strategic objectives were announced which included having the Una as the border of the Serbian state. So on the basis of the strategic objectives, the president of the War Presidency is telling the army or suggesting to the army to cleanse the left bank, destroy as many residential buildings as possible, and fortify the right bank. So military action on the basis of the strategic objectives is being channelled through the War Presidency. I would also note quickly, we might not have much time in the military section, that a month earlier, in April, Klickovic was writing orders to the police, now that the -- to the military. Now that the army has been established it's a proposal, so not a direct order, but it's still clearly conveying policy and trying to have it implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2616, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the last document in relation to Crisis Staffs receiving orders and implementing policies from the republic level is 65 ter 05844.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a presidential decision on return of resettled persons to the territory of the Serbian Republic dated the 2nd of June, 1992, and published in the Official Gazette on the 8th of June, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The English is the wrong decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's actually 172. This was supposed to be corrected in e-court, the English translation -- okay. Just reading from the -- oh, here we go --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Down at the bottom of the English.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you explain the significance of this decision.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's a Presidency decision which grants municipal Crisis Staffs a great deal of authority in determining the status of the -- on the -- people who have left the territory of the Serbian Republic and whether they can return, whether they'll even be granted citizenship. So clearly the Presidency regards Crisis Staffs as a municipal authority if in this decision published in the gazette they're granting this authority to Crisis Staffs, it's telling people who return to report to their Crisis Staffs. The Crisis Staffs will decide on who has the right to return, who has the right of citizenship, and the Crisis Staffs will take over the -- take care of and use the property of those who do not return. So it's significant for the role of the Crisis Staff as recognised by the Presidency and it's also significant for the role of the Crisis Staff in the -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And without calling it up, it's 65 ter 21251, in July 1992, do you recall them publishing a document which referred to this exhibit that we have on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. A correction was published in the Official Gazette which changed the dates, because as you can see here, the date says they have to return by the 20th of May but the decision is published later than that. However, the text -- the correction does not alter the term "Crisis Staff." It changes the date to July 1992 but that's all, which I take as further indication of the recognition that Crisis Staffs are the municipal authority whatever term they're using at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document, 21251, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you also listed some other documents in appendix B supporting the documents that we have just gone through from appendix A. One of them is 65 ter 23137 -- sorry, 01528, which is the president of the government, Branko Djeric. It's dated the 15th of May, 1992, and it's referred to in footnote 82 of your report --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't memorised the appendix B, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- where he orders the Crisis Staff to supply trucks for transport of prisoners from Pale to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, there's a series that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Visoko --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, there is a series of orders from Djeric to municipalities, Sokolac and Vogosca and elsewhere, on organising -- providing trucks for the transport of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also listed is a decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff regarding membership and functions of municipal War Presidencies and that's dated the 11th of June, 1992, cited in footnote 122 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it shows the ARK Crisis Staff passing on the republic-level instructions on War Presidencies, making it clear their function, their authority in the municipality, their role in the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that document also emphasises the continuity between Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies because it links the two together. It constantly says Crisis Staffs/War Presidencies or Crisis Staffs, that is, War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the last document in appendix B is 65 ter 06668, an order from the president of the Republika Srpska government to the War Presidency of Vogosca, dated the 17th of June, 1992. This is cited in footnote 68 and 82 of your report and it's in relation to securing production operations at Pretis.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's an example of an order from the government to a specific Crisis Staff. We both -- we saw Djeric before ordering Crisis Staffs as a category. Here it's to a specific Crisis Staff on war production at Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can turn now to the issue of financial and material support for Crisis Staffs from the government, this is dealt with in paragraph 61 of your report. You describe in that paragraph the Government of the RS issuing instructions and directions, but did the government materially support the Crisis Staffs in any way; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They did. We see in the minutes of the RS government discussions of loans to specific Crisis Staffs, extending them money. We see in the accounts of Crisis Staffs and their balance sheets that they received cash from the government and used it to pay -- often to pay their soldiers. We also see the government co-ordinating between Crisis Staffs. Apparently Sokolac, I think, controlled a lot of commodity reserves because the government is requesting them to release food for different -- other Crisis Staffs. We see reference to Crisis Staffs members meeting in Pale with the government to get money and equipment for creating a Serbian police station. So we see direct cash, we see food assistance, and other kinds of practical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these are cited in footnote 86 of your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: 85 and 86, yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: All this, to my mind, is further evidence of the role of Crisis Staffs in the state that the government considered its job to support them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In appendix B you refer to five documents there. You mentioned already Trnovo, which is 65 ter 17221. That's in relation to the provision of essential resources, including money, communication, equipment, and cars and radios for the Serbian police station.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, and it refers to an agreement made in Pale two days before. So I would suggest that personal -- after a personal visit they agreed on what they needed and the government said: Well, send a letter of what you need.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also note in that document that the Crisis Staff is saying: Send the money to the SDS municipal board account. It just shows how related those organs are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And 01577 is referred to in footnote 179 of your report. It's a spreadsheet balance of the Ilijas Municipal Assembly for the period 11 May 1992 to 30 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. You see in the revenues money coming in from the government, numbers 1 and 2, and then the expenses, the payments -- many of the payments are to TO commanders and TO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2623, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also in appendix B, document 01552 dated the 1st of June, 1992, a recapitulation of the Vogosca Crisis Staff cashier's office counter transactions between the 1st of May, 1992, and the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Again, the first item is the aid -- the assistance from the SRBH, which I take here to be Serbian Republic of BiH. And the bulk of the payments, as you can see, is soldiers' daily allowance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 2624.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Another document, 65 ter 00159, this is referred to in your report at paragraph 61, footnote 85, it's minutes of a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's referred to in footnote 85, minutes of a meeting of the Bosnian Serb government held on the 18th of May, 1992, and if we could go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does this document -- is the Ministry of Finance charged with anything?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, number 4, the Ministry of Finance is to propose solutions for giving aid, that is, temporary loans, to Crisis Staffs. That's at 30 -- it seems to be if they're aiding 30 Crisis Staffs, they're clearly regarding them as a state organ to be supported.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move now to the Crisis Staffs reporting to the republic-level organs, and if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2625, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 01019 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While that's coming up, did you find any evidence that the Crisis Staffs were reporting back to the state organs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They report -- there's written reports, there's written requests brought to government and Presidency. There's also references to oral reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is -- the document that will be coming on the screen is a report from the Bijeljina Crisis Staff sent to the Main Board on the situation on 1st April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's the Bijeljina SDS Crisis Staff reporting to the SDS Main Board, but I would note that it's 1st of April. It's generally within April, as I say, that we see the transformation, or after the 4th of April, into municipal organs. But they're reporting on the situation in Bijeljina. As we know from the general record, this is the time of the Serbian take-over of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2626, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next document is 00153.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You made reference to this a moment ago. It's the minutes of the session of the National Security Council and the Government of the Republika Srpska BiH held on the 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The National Security Council accepted a report on the work of Crisis Staffs, number 9, and municipal organs of government. So someone is reporting on the work of Crisis Staffs. It's part of the job of the National Security Council, apparently, to review the work of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2627, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 17230 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a report of the Rajlovac Crisis Staff dated the 28th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's addressed to the Serbian government of Bosnia and it seems -- it's reporting on the number of conscripts in the Serbian army of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, which also is an indication of the military role. So it's reporting and reporting on the military role or the military activities of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2628, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And lastly, an example of a War Commission reporting. If we could have P02371 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is referred to in footnote 94 of your report and then paragraph 64. This is recommendation signed by Nikola Poplasen regarding the transformation of the prison in Vogosca into the penal correction facility in Butmir or Pale.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, Poplasen is the commissioner for Vogosca. He's addressing it, if you notice, to the War Presidency of the Serb Republic, indicating that at the highest level the Presidency is also operating in the same way as a War Presidency, and he is saying that the prison in Vogosca is illegal in the view of our legal regulations. So he suggests that it be transformed into a subdivision of the Butmir facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you made reference to the War Presidency, of course this document's dated the 24th of June, 1992, which is after the decision you were talking about on forming the --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I'm referring here that it's addressed to the republican level. The War Presidency is the Expanded Presidency operating at the republic level. It's not the municipal War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now go to an Assembly session on the 24th of November, 1992, and that's Exhibit P01105. And I want to deal very, very briefly with this document. If we could go, please, to page 100 to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was discussed in -- at this Assembly session in relation to war commissioners?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This whole Assembly session -- not this whole, but this part of the debate in the Assembly is on the question of War Commissions and whether they're constitutional, whether they should amend the constitution or abolish those bodies. And here Krajisnik is saying -- if you recall, I note in my report Krajisnik was the member of the Presidency responsible for the work of commissioner. He's saying he knew very well what the commissioners were doing --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, if I can just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The B/C/S is on page 97 and it starts at ERN 0214-9728. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, if you can continue.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I don't see it in the B/C/S, but he's saying that he knows very well what the commissioner -- how the commissioners did their job and they did them very efficiently. I see it on page 102 of the English -- I'm sorry, what do you want me to see on page 100 here?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was starting the --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's the beginning of the discussion --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- the discussion about the war commissioners.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it goes on for some 11 pages in the English and from page 97 to 109 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I would ask you to go to page 102 in the English. In the B/C/S 0214-9731. He's saying in the English that they worked very efficiently and well. I know that every deputy who went provided great service. He's saying how well -- he knows how well the commissioners did. He says: [No interpretation]. [In English] Just saying that he was on top of it, he knew where everyone was going and he names them. Further on in the debate there's more discussion of how well the commissioners worked and that they received oral instructions and that -- as well as the written kind we've seen. So this debate shows us that the commissioners were working and they were reporting and transmitting information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to Mijatovic speaking on page 108 of the English and it's on page 0214-9737 of the B/C/S. In your report you have made reference to this at footnote 96. If we can see in the English there are illegible words there. If you can just read out that sentence that Mr. Mijatovic is saying in relation to "I make the following motion ... I no longer feel like a commissioner ..." That sentence there -- starting there.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it in the -- yes, thanks. Could you make it a little larger for me. It says: [Interpretation] "I will send a report to the president who appointed me ..." [In English] It's quite legible in the B/C/S. I don't know why it's marked illegible here, and I take that as a clear statement of the commissioner feeling his duty is to report to the president which has appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so as we have seen over the documents that we have just shown from April 1992 of the Crisis Staffs reporting up to the republic level, what is the importance of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Overall, not just this one? Yes, it's -- I find ample evidence that the Crisis Staffs regarded themselves and were regarded as part of the Bosnian Serb state system, and part of their job was receiving orders and reporting back, and I see evidence of all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to briefly talk about the regional Crisis Staffs, and this is dealt with in your report at paragraph 30 and also 57 and 59. We've had a couple of documents or at least one from Birac, but we've talked about the municipal Crisis Staffs being established at the regional level. Can you just briefly explain the establishment of the regional level Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As I say in my report, I don't talk much about them because the document record is so unbalanced. There is a great deal of evidence from ARK, there is very little from the other regions, so I'm hesitant to draw any pattern. What we do see is that similar to the municipal level, crisis -- a regional Crisis Staff was formed as the -- with the authority of the regional Assembly and similarly saw itself as part of the Bosnian Serb state system, a small collective body acting in place of the Assembly. Beyond that, as I say, I'm very hesitant because it's so scattered, the documentary evidence, beyond ARK. ARK is so robust, it appears that the other regions were not as robust, but where we do have documents such as the one from Birac, they clearly see themselves as part of the state system.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the role of the regional Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Was to co-ordinate defence to pass on -- to be the first stop for municipalities to address their concerns before going to the republic level, to co-ordinate defence and other efforts over the entire region. Beyond that, I see so little aside from ARK that I don't want to even say what their duties were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff receive orders from the RS government organs and did they act upon them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they received them, acted upon them, and passed them on to the municipal level, as we saw in the case of the decision on War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this is in footnote 101 of your report. I want to turn now to the military role of the Crisis Staffs. What role, if any, did the Crisis Staffs play in the municipal take-overs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They led the take-overs, they co-ordinated all the forces of coercion involved in -- the armed forces in the take-overs where there was a military -- where force was involved, they declared themselves to be the municipal authorities and therefore took over the government positions in the municipality. They were the van -- they planned and led the take-overs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the level of co-operation and co-ordination between the Crisis Staff and the military, what was that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Very close. A -- the commander of the military forces was a member of the Crisis Staff. Actions were discussed in the Crisis Staff. The military was told what to do, although it may not be ordered exactly how to carry out the tasks. It was at the very minimum co-ordination, communication, bringing all the forces together into one body. In some places, as I say in my report, we see the Crisis Staffs actually ordering specific units, but it's a -- it's a spectrum of relationships. The minimum is them all meeting and collectively deciding on the take-over, including the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And one example, if we could call up 65 -- and this is in appendix B - 01023. This is a report from the Bijeljina SJB, the public security station, on the overall security situation in Bijeljina municipality and the SAO Semberija and Majevica. It's dated the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is in appendix B, the -- the -- maybe in the other binder beside you.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Do you have the footnote? I know the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Footnote 69, 73, 80, and 120 in your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It says that the TO and the Serbian Volunteer Guard under the direction of the Crisis Staff took over the -- it's just at the bottom of the English page if we could have the next page as well. "During the night and the next day, the TO," could we have the next page in the English, "Serbian National Guard and Serbian Volunteer Guard removed the barricades under the supervision of the Bijeljina Crisis Staff." So that's their description of the take-over. The Serbian Volunteer Guard, I would note, is the name for Arkan's units, were being directed -- supervised by the Crisis Staff. It's more -- the B/C/S is [B/C/S/ spoken] which is a little more direct than supervision, it's the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Another one on the 65 ter -- on appendix B, sorry, is 65 ter 07685. This is a Radio Prijedor broadcast of 29 April 1995 of an interview conducted with Simo Miskovic, Slobodan Kuruzovic, Milan Kovacevic about the take-over of the Prijedor municipality on the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they described the co-operation with the JNA -- the -- Colonel Arsic. They describe how they met on the weekend to -- as to -- to take over, how it was planned, and Arsic -- and Zeka is Colonel-Major Zeljaja. I don't know if you have one particular quotation, but the whole account is a very good description of the actual take-over of Prijedor, and they mention the Crisis Staff having previously been established as a shadow government and then just steps up with the help of the JNA here and the TO and the police to take over power.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the previous one, 1023?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I thought exhibit -- oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 01023 will be Exhibit P2629 and 07685 will be Exhibit P2630.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you list in footnote 136 other examples of the level of co-operation and co-ordination between the Crisis Staff and the military. But I just want to just ask you a question or two in relation to the Crisis Staffs and the TOs. You deal with this in paragraph 69 of your report and also in paragraph 72. You talk about the instructions stipulated co-operation between the Crisis Staff and the commands.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The TO or the JNA, paragraph 72 is referring to the JNA more. But the TO -- the difference was, of course, that the JNA was the established Yugoslav army. The TOs were municipality-based. The constitution provided that municipalities or the municipal authorities organised their TOs. So with Crisis Staffs operating as municipal authorities, they in some places formed their own TOs or put -- would put their men in charge of the municipal TO command, and the TO commander was part of the Crisis Staff. And we see a lot of orders issued by Crisis Staffs to TOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the Crisis Staff's level of involvement, if any, in the arming of the local Serbs and the formation of Serbian units?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It depends very much on the situation in each municipality, and unfortunately secret arming isn't the kind of thing that I see a lot of documentary evidence about, but I do see references to it in SDS minutes and in reports on the Crisis Staff, for example, that I think it's in Krupa that they single out the people who did the most to arm the Serbs, members of the Crisis Staff who did the most to arm Serbs before the war. So Crisis Staffs were certainly involved in it. I would have to look at each municipality to describe a pattern because as Karadzic himself said in his speech on how the army -- the SDS created the army, in some places they had the co-operation of the JNA and in some places they had to hide from the JNA, so that's why it's hard to describe one pattern for creating armies and TOs -- armed units and TOs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I want to deal now with the relationship between the Crisis Staffs and paramilitaries. You refer to this in paragraph 75 of your report. What was the relationship?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Again, it's not something that there's one single pattern or that I found evidence of everywhere, but certainly some Crisis Staffs invited paramilitaries, groups from elsewhere in Bosnia and from Serbia, paid them, gave them material support, used them as their own forces. Materiel?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter -- this is an example that was in appendix B, 65 ter 02553, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a Zvornik interim government decision dated the 4th of May, 1992. Can you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I would just note here that, for one thing, Zvornik is an odd exception, in that their municipal -- their small collective emergency municipal Presidency was called the interim government, but the Crisis Staff became the interim government. And here they are paying 10.000 or 10 million dinars -- 10.000, I guess, to what they call the volunteers from Loznica to be paid to their commander, Zuca. This was a notorious group of volunteers in Zvornik, the Yellow Wasps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, do we have a document in which we can see the establishment of interim government in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's cited in my report. I do note that it was an exception and it was the Crisis Staff in early April and then becomes the interim government, but I'm not sure that I cite here that -- a document that shows the relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's the conclusion -- your conclusion based upon the documents you have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- been observing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the documents of the Zvornik provisional government are published in their municipal gazette, so it's quite clearly operating as the municipal authority. I would have to consult the gazette if they have the decisions of the Crisis Staff first, but it's the only place where I see this term used instead of "Crisis Staff" or "Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. B/C/S word doesn't end with e.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 65 ter 01781 -- oh, sorry, which is D00325.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just noticed one more thing on this document I never really noticed it, but it says -- it looks like it was received. It says [Interpretation] "Received by," [In English] and then, well, it looks like it could be Zuca. Sorry, I hadn't noticed that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we can go now to D00325 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, this is the report entitled "Analysis of the Combat-readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992" referred to in paragraph 82 of your report and footnote 133.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to, I think, page 10, pages 10 and 13 of the English and pages 11 and 13 of the B/C/S. First of all page 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The paragraph at the bottom of page 10 in the B -- in the English describes the process that I describe in my report, that originally the units were -- many of them commanded by Crisis Staffs, but as the Army of Republika Srpska was established it took over the command of those units. So it says there's two stages, the first from April 1st to June 15th, and in the first period describes the self organising of municipal and other regional units on the basis of Territorial Defence units under the political and patriotic influence of the Serbian Democratic Party. And they operated within the municipalities and stopped at that, he says. Well, the next reference makes it explicitly Crisis Staffs, but clearly they're organised at the municipal level, commanded at the municipal level in the beginning, for the period here cited as 1st April to 15 June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 13 of the English and page 13 also of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the section 1.1, again noting the establishment of the VRS, it says the infantry units were used at the beginning of the war according to the decisions of Crisis Staffs and similar authoritative bodies. And when the Army of Republika Srpska was formed these units were incorporated into it, while in places where there were no units of the former JNA, they were the foundation for the establishment of infantry units. So that's the process I describe in my report, where first there were self-organised units led by the Crisis -- led by the SDS and the -- commanded by Crisis Staffs which were then incorporated into the VRS when it was formed. In some places where there were no JNA units, these new units were made up on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in paragraph 81 of your report you say that some Crisis Staffs were prepared to interpret the government and party instructions in a manner giving them authority, and you give examples in footnote 129. If we can just look at a couple of examples. The first one is from Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 00574, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicate in my report, it's a spectrum with the most assertive or the most military end of the spectrum being the Crisis Staff directly commanding units. And we see this here in the first paragraph in Vlasenica. It's a report from 1994 on the formation of the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, and it says: On the 20th of April 1992, the forces of the JNA and already formed units led by the Crisis Staff of the SDS liberated Vlasenica. And then -- and the SDS Crisis Staff mobilised men from the former TO on the 21st of April. Then further down it says: The SDS Crisis Staff commanded and controlled detachments in the field through their established staff for command and control until the 28th of June, 1992, when all the units became part of the 1st Bircanski Brigade. So that's an example of the process I describe, SDS setting up its own -- commanding its forces which eventually are incorporated into the now being created VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so during that time, what impact, if any, did the formation of the VRS have on the interaction between the Crisis Staffs and the military?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: We see it has here the Crisis Staffs integrating their units into the VRS as its being established. We see VRS commanders coming to Crisis Staffs -- being part of the Crisis Staff, participating in Crisis Staff sessions. We see certainly continued co-ordination, co-operation, support, the Crisis Staffs are still responsible for, for example, mobilisation and getting the recruits into these units, supporting these units, materially. But throughout June into July we see the VRS taking a more assertive role in command. We see even some discussion of conflict. The military thinks the Crisis Staff has in some places overstepped their authority and there's some places where the Crisis Staffs don't seem willing to hand it -- give up their units oro their command as easily, but it's definitely -- it's a transition which generally by the end of July, the VRS is robust enough to be commanding the units. But everyone acknowledges that many of them were originally commanded by the Crisis Staffs. We see that in the Rogatica -- it's not in the appendix but in Rogatica they say: Even though we formed the VRS that doesn't mean our jobs have changed. Our job is still to support the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And one document you have in appendix B is the conclusions of the Vogosca Crisis Staff meeting held on the 16th of May. The document's dated the 17th of May, that's 65 ter 01534, where I think in that document the Crisis Staff were asserting a military role. This is in footnote 165 and 169 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Certainly in Vogosca, the Crisis Staff head Jovan Tintor said he was military and civilian commander. He was quite assertive of his military role. And here the Crisis Staff is ordering the take-over of the army barracks in Semizovac and placing them under the command of the Crisis Staff which is under the sole command of the Serbian Republic of BiH. I would note also that item 2 here describes the cleansing, the "ciscenje," of Svrake and Semizovac. And item 5, dismisses the Muslim and Croatian employees from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the Court, please, the meaning of the word "ciscenje" and how it's referred to in different terms in documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: "Cistiti" means "to clean." "Ciscenje" means "cleaning" or "cleansing." "Ciscenje terena" can mean "mopping-up operations." But "etnicko ciscenje" means "ethnic cleansing." So I think we found it preferable when we see the word "cistiti" or "ciscenje" to leave it in the original with -- so that the meaning can be determined from the context, whether it's simply a mopping up of the terrain, a military term for the final stages of an operation, or whether it refers to ethnic cleansing, the forcible removal of the population. Here it simply says "cleansing" in quotation marks which is unusual, I would say, in the original B/C/S. So I just note it's left also -- the second usage here is left just "cleansed" in the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we're discussing the language, if we could look at another document on appendix B, 65 ter 17231, it's a letter from the Rajlovac War Commission to Republika Srpska Presidency dated the 2nd of July, 1992. It's referred to in footnote 90 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This is another use of the word "cleansing," "ciscenje," where fighters from the Brijesce settlement have written a letter to the War Commission which then forwards it to the Presidency saying: It's up for you to decide. We're not in charge of deciding the cleansing, the "ciscenje." But they're requiring the "ciscenje" of Brijesce. If we could have the English up, or is it not in English yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that there's no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will have that uploaded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime we haven't given the number for Vlasenica document, which is 54 -- 574. You are tendering it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document, 17231.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask whether this is all because no mention is made here of "ciscenje," cleansing, so might we have the entire document displayed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I would also like to see the English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have this document which is signed, because we've seen quite a number of documents today with no signature and no number? So the attached letter does have a number but not the first document. Regardless of the fact that in the main letter there's no mention of snipers and combat, so cleansing, "ciscenje," as a military term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't -- that's the only version of the letter I've seen. This signed thing that's now on the screen is not related to that. Oh, but that -- the -- yes, this -- the -- this first thing is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we come back to this document later on when we have English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have it -- no, I don't have the English translation in my binder either. No, I'm sorry. We just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hesitate to interrupt the examination-in-chief, but all documents not signed and given a reference number are unacceptable as far as the Defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can object when this document is tendered and that may be a good subject for your cross-examination if admitted. We'll carry on in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next document I would like to quickly look at is, it's already an exhibit, P01493. It's a letter from the commander of the VS in BiH Ilijas Ratko Adzic to the president of the Presidency, dated the 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were talking about different ends of the spectrum a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. I would put this at the more military end of the spectrum because the letter-head says the command of the Ilijas -- the Serbian army of Ilijas. It's sent to the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic and he's informing him on the defence lines, that they're holding the defence lines. And he asks for tanks and self-propelled anti-aircraft guns to cleanse certain areas, that's "ocistim terena" [phoen], so it refers to the phrase "cleansing of terrain." And Ratko Adzic, who is the president of the municipality, president of the Crisis Staff, member of the SDS Main Board, here signs himself as commander of the army of the Serbian people of Ilijas. So he's clearly directly involved in the military effort, calling himself a commander and asking for tanks and guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think the other end of the spectrum would be the Kljuc Crisis Staff which you've referred to in paragraph 80 of your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, Kljuc I might put a little more in the middle, in that they told them -- gave themselves permission to wear uniforms and carry arms, so they clearly see themselves as having a military role. But they state clearly that they will issue orders to the military but they will not interfere in the way the orders are carried out. So that is, I think, sort of the middle -- the clear definition of the relationship. The War Presidency will issue the orders, the military will not be interfered -- will not be micro-managed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did the government make any recommendations with respect to military matters in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the things I noted at -- in late May the VRS has been established although it's still in formation, but the army is now seen as able to take over the defence. So the recommendation -- the government recommends on the 23rd of May that Crisis Staffs be abolished. The minutes on the 21st of May make it clear that that is connected to the army's ability to take over defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I won't bring those documents up, but that's the -- the minutes of the meeting of the government on the 21st of May is 65 ter 00160, and the 23rd of May is 65 ter 00161.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, they're the subject of a bar table motion at the moment. I just note that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to discuss the Crisis Staff relations with the police force and you dealt with that in paragraphs 87 to 94 of your report. With respect to the police, were the ties between the police and the Crisis Staffs any different from those of the military?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I would say they were even closer because the police were municipality-based. We see the 19 December instructions already involving the -- telling the Crisis Staff to take over the police stations. We see Crisis Staffs helping set up the new Serbian police stations, materially supporting, that is, getting equipment, uniforms, and other things for the police forces. The commander of the police or the police station is a member of the Crisis Staff. We see many orders from Crisis Staffs to the police. So it's clearer I would say and closer -- more easily defined than the one between the Crisis Staff and the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Karadzic say about the relationship between the police and the new Serb authorities at the 12th Assembly Session on the 24th of March, 1992; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, he describes the taking over of the municipality and the -- or part of it is separating the police and setting up a Serbian police, and he says quite clearly the police will be under the civilian authority. It must obey it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But are the -- were there also parallel chains of command?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, because the police did have their own ministry, so there were parallel chains of command in that the police also consulted with minister -- the regional ministry officials up to the level of the minister, but as we see the Expanded Presidency, the War Presidency at the republic level included the minister of the interior. So the lines -- we have at the highest level the military police party government coming together and then repeated at the municipal level. So we see Crisis Staffs ordering police forces. Occasionally the police force consulting the higher level or having their -- the Crisis Staff decisions confirmed, but never being told: Don't carry that out because the Crisis Staff has no authority. Similarly to the military, we see by July the police having a sufficiently robust structure that they're saying the Crisis Staff should back down. They have ordered them in the past, but now we don't like that interference, but it's certainly not what we're seeing in April, for example. And the Crisis Staffs -- or, sorry, the evidence stresses even in July the commonality of purpose. Roles are getting more clearly defined, but the role of the police is to make sure that the municipality is secure so that the Crisis Staff can run the municipality. And always the commander of the police was a member of the Crisis Staff which operated collectively, so he would be part of the decision-making when the orders would be drafted for the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You cite in paragraph 91 of your report - I won't take you to the documents - and in footnotes 148 and 149 you're giving examples of where the Serb police forces were created and there was co-ordination in reporting between the Crisis Staff and the municipal police forces in relation to the disarming of the non-Serb population, for example. And where in paragraph 94 you describe the level or degree first of the issuing of orders and then receiving reports from municipal SJBs.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is there any other further comment you wish to make on that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, we have seen, for example, from Prijedor and other places, a list of orders carried out by the police. And when you read Crisis Staff minutes, the commander's always there -- the commander of the police is always part of the Crisis Staffs contributing and one of the documents I cite is the diary of the police commander in Krupa is meeting almost every day with the Crisis Staff president. The co-operation is very close. The orders are carried out. It's quite clear the relationship there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The one you just talked about then, the Prijedor police station, that's 65 ter number, that's on appendix B, 05767, dated the 1st of July. It's a list of all the municipal and regional Crisis Staff decisions which were implemented by the police. Is that the document you were referring to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to have that document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what we are seeing now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a number, but I'd like to see the signature, nonetheless, on page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I want to turn now to talk about the actions of the Crisis Staffs in municipalities and that's dealt with at paragraphs 95 to 106 of your report. In paragraph 97 you state: "The status and exodus of non-Serbs in Serb municipalities was a constant theme of the Crisis Staff's work." And I want to now just take you to a few examples of the actions of the Crisis Staffs in relation to the non-Serb population. I want to deal very quickly with 65 ter 11505. This is a resolution dated the 23rd of July, 1992, by the Celinac War Presidency on the status of the non-Serb population on the territory of the county of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. It gives the non-Serbs a special status with, it says, clearly expressed rights and responsibilities, but in fact those are restrictions. If we can see the next page, it's a pretty restrictive status they have, such as -- Article 5, forbidden from moving around certain times, forbidden from lingering in the street, forbidden from swimming in the rivers, hunting, and fishing, travelling without permission. Article 4, you notice it's organising their departure, which is another common theme we'll see. I think there might be more on the next page of their -- of the English of their restrictions. No more than three men can gather in a group, contacting relations who are not in Celinac, communications systems aside from the public telephone, from using cars. So the very fact that the Crisis Staff feels it can issue an order like this on the status of certain of its citizens is very telling about the authority and the jobs that it saw for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is quite a strongly worded document. Did you see or have you seen any evidence of anybody speaking against this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, I know it was -- there was some effort to publish it in the West when it was exposed. There was -- I saw references in 1993 when the Municipal Assembly is trying -- is meeting for the first time and has to verify the decisions, they -- this one is really bad, we can't accept this one, but I see no -- I see no objection raised at the time from higher-ups in ARK or at the republic level. I see no condemnation of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in footnotes 167 of your report, there's other examples of Crisis Staffs controlling the freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, similar things are not moving from your village, not gathering in groups, it's a theme of the authority of the Crisis Staff and the municipality controlling freedom of movement. Not everywhere is explicitly applying only to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to paragraph 96 of your report where you state that in various Crisis Staffs -- in various cases Crisis Staffs variously established, controlled and supported detention centres. Can you just briefly describe the types of orders issued by the Crisis Staff in this regard.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Some Crisis Staffs named places to be set up as detention centres, some Crisis Staffs named the kind of people they wanted arrested, such as all military-aged Muslims who could possibly harm the Serbs or put all Croats in special facilities, send -- they made lists of people to be sent to some of the most notorious camps such as Manjaca. They said Serbs who have been imprisoned by mistake should be released. So it's pretty clear their discriminatory intentions and the role of the Crisis Staffs in making -- in establishing detention centres in their municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can tender the Celinac document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P2638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we know who signed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's typed-signed with the War Presidency. I don't see a handwritten signature. It has a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to decipher the stamp?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Not in -- if I could have it enlarged. The translation indicates that there is some signature, but I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just looking back at that last answer, the witness indicated that their discriminatory intentions were pretty clear. I think that we have been in the past not accepting evidence of other people's intentions, particularly came up in your absence in one instance recently. And I don't know that it's necessary to strike that - you've already heard it and you're professional Judges - but we would at least like to point out that we don't believe that it's the proper role of an expert to be speculating on other persons' intentions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't how I understood Ms. Hanson's evidence. She was referring to Crisis Staffs and she, in her report, footnotes to documents which shows the Crisis Staffs' decisions relating to the non-Serb population. And from that evidence, Ms. Hanson is making this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, the proper weight can be given by the Judges. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you -- if we could have Exhibit -- sorry, in paragraph 93 of your report you refer to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP report, footnote 153 and 156 on report of some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead, which is addressed to the president of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, and the prime minister, dated the 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have that exhibit, P01096, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very quickly can you explain -- if we can go to page 3 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The police are saying that the army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies are ordering the arrest of as many Muslim civilians as they can. At the top of page 3 in the B/C/S - yes - and in the English as well. "The army, Crisis Staffs, and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs." So I cite that as an example of Crisis Staffs ordering detention of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to another document, 65 ter 04200, it's a decision of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most Crisis Staff containing information on the categorisation of persons sent to Manjaca camp, dated the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the document you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, where they say that -- under item 1, Roman numeral III, among the people being sent are people who are not welcome in the territory of Sanski Most. They list politicians, national extremists, and people unwelcome to be sent to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2639, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the next document is 65 ter 05751.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's referred to in paragraph 96 of your report. It's an order of the Prijedor public security station chief, dated the 31st of May, 1992. And again, very briefly, the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. The police are acting following a decision of the Crisis Staff, the chief of police is ordering that Omarska mine compound be used as a collection centre. So it's the police implementing a decision of the Crisis Staff, setting up one of the most notorious collect -- detention camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2640, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 99 of your report you state that the Crisis Staffs carried out the policies and procedures for the forcible departure of non-Serbs, and in footnotes 169 to 171 you provide examples of Crisis Staffs actually setting forced deportation as policy. If we could look at a couple of documents in that regard, 65 ter 00821. This is conclusions adopted at a subregional meeting of the political representatives of the municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc, of the 7th of June, 1992. Can you very briefly tell us what the significance of this document is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, I note on the first page that it's sent to the ARK Crisis Staff and to the leadership of the Serbian Republic. They're asking in a couple of items for clear instructions -- clear policy from above on things such as the corridor, the borders. But if we could go to the next page they are saying that they want to move out -- move the non-Serbs out in order to establish Serbian power. It says, item number 6: "All municipalities in our subregion agree that the Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities to a level where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory ..." So the municipalities agree to maintain Serbian power the Muslims and Croats should be moved out -- or move out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another document quickly from appendix B, it's 65 ter 07254. It's in relation to the Foca municipality. It's dated the 18th of June, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I once again -- could Ms. Sutherland tell us who signed this document? Because anybody can write something like this, but someone needs to sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It says it's stamped. Can you see the last page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As Mr. Karadzic can see for himself, the document is not signed. It does have a stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we -- I believe it's the SDS stamp. If we could go back to that document, I could read it. Yes, it's the stamp of the SDS Municipal Board of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no name of the responsible person issuing it nor is there a signature --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- how come?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a subject --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a matter for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have document 07254 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a letter of the Foca War Commission to operative staff and executive committee dated the 18th of June, 1992. It's cited in footnote 9 -- footnotes 98 and 177 of your report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, and it says that the War Commission has discussed with the -- here translated as "government envoy" but the original B/C/S is "povjerenik," the government commissioner, they've discussed the issue of the moving out of the Muslims, that the Muslims want to move out. So I take that to mean that the war commissioner appointed by the government was familiar with the situation in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are these conclusions made in consultation with representatives of the BH Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: That's what they -- it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
