utterances.text: That will be P2642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, in paragraphs 100 and 101 you discuss the removal of non-Serbs from the territory, and in footnote 172 you provide examples of committees for immigration and travel agencies and exchange offices established by the Crisis Staffs. In paragraph 101 you talk about the criteria, the Crisis Staff criteria, for departure. What was the general criteria, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The general criteria was that they sign a form stating that they were leaving voluntarily and handing over their property to the municipality, and the municipality would arrange their departure in buses usually, or convoys. Another criteria was paying a fee and in some cases limiting the amount of money they could take with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in paragraph 102 of your report you talk about the systematic collection and redistribution of non-Serb property.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, those who were leaving were told they could only leave if they sign their property over to the state or the property of those who had left was declared now municipal property.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The last document I want to show you is 65 ter 00855, and this is referred to in paragraph 99 and in footnotes 79, 140, 161, 166, 168, and 169 of your report. It's the report of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff (War Presidency) of the work of the Crisis Staff for the period since 15th of May, 1992, and it's dated the 29th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The first --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, in reference to the title Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies, the fact that these names are used together, again what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It indicates to me the continuity seen between these two organs, which the text on the next page makes quite clear when they discuss the sessions of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could quickly go through this document and if you can highlight for the Chamber the important paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, the first paragraph says that the Crisis Staff was established on 23 December. We saw those minutes. The third paragraph describes how it held earlier sessions as an organ of the SDS, then four sessions before hostilities, 16 sessions during the war, three sessions as War Presidency, so it describes the continuity. It says on the basis of the Presidency decision of 31 May it was established as a War Presidency. So that's the implementation of the decision we saw. It says it bases its work on collective work, which I've noted before. They met every day when necessary. If I could see the next page of the English to catch up with what I'm saying, and the next page of the B/C/S as well now, where it says that the army participate -- regularly participated, that all major questions related to army and police were resolved within the Crisis Staff. So it makes it very clear the role of the Crisis Staff and the military. It says: Very good co-operation between the Crisis Staff and military organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think on -- are we on page 5?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Not yet, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does this document also discuss the relocation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. It says that the status of Muslim citizens were dealt with and the organised moving out of Muslims was decided by -- at the Crisis Staff session. So the very status of Muslims was a topic for the Crisis Staff and the Crisis Staff organised the moving out of the Muslims. And it also -- the paragraph above, I note simply that they reviewed the conclusions of the regional Crisis Staff which were binding to their work as well. So then they dealt with personnel issues in the court and elsewhere. I discuss that in my report as well, how Crisis Staffs would appoint Serbs to the courts and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on page 7 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S we can see that it's type-signed the Crisis Staff War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2643, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you -- in your report at paragraphs 103 to 114 you deal with War Presidencies between 1993 and 1994. And then in paragraphs 115 to 141 you deal with War Presidencies between 1994 and 1995. In paragraph 135 you state that the available documentation on municipal War Presidencies in the latter period, 1994/1995, is much scantier than for 1992, but for records found to date indicate that the later War Presidencies operated within the RS state system in a manner consistent with the earlier bodies. Briefly, what were the chief differences, if any, between the earlier Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies of 1992 and the later bodies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The ones from 1994 and 1995 are well defined. The ones from 1993 are uncertain enough that I won't speak to that now. The main difference would be the role of the military. By then obviously the VRS was thoroughly established, and the military role of the Crisis Staff -- of the War Presidencies were expressly limited. The military representation of the War Presidencies was at a lower level, it was an assistant commander usually. So it's not a command position. The War Presidencies are supporting the military effort, but their direct military role is strictly limited. And there is thorough discussion in the Assemblies on these -- the legislation for these War Presidencies. There are guide-lines issued by the government. It's -- the whole state was functioning much more clearly by then and the difference can be seen in War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your conclusions are at paragraphs 142 to 147 of the report. What does all the available evidence present in respect -- in respect to a pattern, if any?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: That Crisis Staffs were created to establish Serbian power in municipalities on the ground, that they carried out those, and in doing that, those objectives -- in doing so, they helped create the Serbian state on the ground and were part of the Bosnian Serb state system, considered themselves as such, were seen as such by the higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And at paragraph 144 you talk about the Crisis Staffs executing the policies --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, as part of the state system they're carrying out the policies of the leadership. That's part of their job as a state organ. They received orders, instructions from the top level; they reported back to the top level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The English has been uploaded for 65 ter 17231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you take a look now. We wanted to find the word "cleansing" there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on the next -- the letter that they sent. It's not on this page. It's the next page. In the second paragraph, the soldiers are complaining that they've heard that Brijesce will not be cleansed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what was your objection, Mr. Karadzic, on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the cover letter, Your Excellency, has all the attributes of an official document. This could have been added by anyone. We can't see it's authentic. There's no signature. There's no typed name, there's no number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, again that may be a subject of your cross-examination. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2644, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your report, as you know, is one of the pillars of this indictment and the Defence has the important task to shed light on everything in the report and how it was made. In view of the very few hours that we were granted, I will have to start with the most important things first. In paragraphs 95 to 107 you suggested that the expulsion of the non-Serbian population was carried out by the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs through Crisis Staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I say that the Crisis Staffs are carrying out the expulsion of the non-Serb population and that they are part of the -- they are -- they see themselves as executing the policies of the leadership. I do not claim that they had specific -- I do not cite any specific orders from the leadership on the expulsion. But I describe what the Crisis Staffs were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You ascribe to the Crisis Staffs many misdeeds, especially expulsion, in times of chaos, that is to say, before the state authorities of the Bosnian Serb state acquired stability and authority, as you say in your paragraph 146 in the conclusions. In that paragraph you make the distinction between the early days and the later days of the war.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The later years of the war. That paragraph is discussing the last -- referring to the last section of the report on 1994/1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you enumerate a number of municipalities randomly, citing individual documents in certain paragraphs which could make the Chamber believe -- although in some places you say you dare not claim there was a pattern and in other places you say there was a pattern. Today in the examination-in-chief, to my great regret, while interpreting and representing certain documents you made things even more difficult for the Defence because you were selective and you were not able to represent the whole document properly, which creates additional difficulties for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's start with Foca, P2642 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was just objecting to the lengthy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the question is coming. Let's start with Foca, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P2642. It was displayed not long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we deal with this specific issue of Foca, would you like to comment on his observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My choice of municipalities was certainly not random. It was directed by the evidence. Where I found evidence, I cited it. When I say there was not a pattern, I was referring mostly to the military -- question of military relations. I made it clear that that's the one area in which I do not find one consistent pattern but I do see a spectrum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I have to put to you a few general questions. Is it the case that first you were an investigator and how did it come about that you became an expert?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I was never an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on that paper shown to us by this woman, Mrs. Sutherland, it says you had worked previously in the OTP section of investigations. You are an officer of the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I work in the OTP. My job is a research officer. Investigations -- investigators are a very different job. I'm a research officer, that's essentially an analyst. I work -- that -- until recently that -- my team, the LRT, fell under the overall section of investigations; it no longer does. But I was never an investigator. That's a specific term within the OTP. I'm a research officer. I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is a researcher also an expert?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Those are two different things. A researcher can be, as I have become, an expert in this topic and appear as an expert witness, but certainly not every researcher -- not every research officer is a court -- is an expert in the terms of the court. We become -- we are knowledgeable about certain subjects, you could call it an expertise. But the court term "expert" is something different from a research officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a witness, do you feel under obligation to be unbiased and comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As a witness, it is my obligation to tell the truth as I see it, the whole truth. Comprehensive? It's not my job to explain the entire course of the war, to describe what the other side did. I am comprehensive in reporting my findings, as comprehensive as time allows. Comprehensive, it's hard to be when we're limited by time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you limited in any way by the Prosecution -- by your connection with the Prosecution? Do you share their views? Your report relies on the indictment and the findings of other employees of the OTP, or does the indictment follow from your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I do not rely on the indictment. I do not rely on other findings of the employees of the OTP except one very specific paragraph, I'm sorry I didn't mention before. I did in earlier testimony. One paragraph relies on one colleague's research, but I absolutely accept it as mine and am responsible for it. That's the paragraph 12 on the legislative background. That is the only time I have relied on another OTP employee. But my report, as I said before, started back in 2001; so if anything, the indictment relies on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that errors in the indictment would follow from errors in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I don't know of errors in my report other than those that I have brought to the Court's attention. I don't know of errors in the indictment. I really in writing this report ignored the indictment. It was not -- it was not in -- to maintain my objectivity, to maintain my distance from the trial team, I was not privy to -- certainly not privy to the drafting of the indictment. I don't -- I may have seen it but I didn't study it for this report. I really don't think there's a relationship between my report and the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I find it hard to believe that you have not read the indictment. It was issued in 1996 and you started your work in 2001. But let me ask you something else. In your efforts to be comprehensive, thorough, have you used all the documents and have you put the stress on and used exculpatory documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Of course I have not used all documents. I reviewed tens of thousands of documents, as I indicated in my examination-in-chief. For each of the examples cited, I could probably supply a half-dozen others. I chose those that I felt were the most succinct, the most telling, the most representative documents. When I encountered exculpatory documents, I passed them to the notice of the trial lawyers, as is my obligation. I did not find a pattern of documentation that I ignored. If I found a pattern of documents indicating that the Crisis Staffs weren't doing something, I would either have included it in my report or just simply made that topic not part of my report. There was much on the work of Crisis Staffs I ignored, their relations with the administrative bodies of the Executive Board and things like that, because it's rather tedious municipal matters. I could have written an entire report on fuel and commodity reserves, but that was not, I felt, relevant. So I did not include all documents. I included all those that I felt to be relevant and representative, and I read widely before I selected; and therefore made my selections on the basis of the patterns that I saw in my wide reading of Crisis Staff documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, were they representative of the guilt, the culpability of the Serbian side, or representative of the entire broad picture, why would you give exculpatory documents to the trial team? Why didn't you incorporate them in your report, as you did with incriminating documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I might find individual exculpatory documents referring to specific events, and it's my obligation as a member of the OTP to bring those to notice, to pass them on. If it was exculpatory -- it could be exculpatory in any manner, not necessarily in my report. But I show here where I see the pattern -- where I see the exceptions to the pattern and I note them. So it's not -- my report -- I don't think I make a judgement on the question of guilt. It's not my job to say who's guilty or who's culpable. I am conveying what I find in the documents, and I am conveying what I find to be the general pattern and I note exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that your report is not complete and that one must take into account that the Prosecutor or trial lawyers have documents that are exculpatory or that they have documents that are exculpatory for municipalities in which the picture was different, more favourable to the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As far as I know, any documents I noted as potentially exculpatory in this research and in all my research I bring to the attention of the lawyers. As far as I know, they disclose them for the relevant cases. I don't believe - if that's what you're asking - that they're sitting on exculpatory documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But why did you not point to those documents in your report? Why didn't you refer to them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Um -- you mean -- what I found was -- formed the basis of my conclusions. As I say, I don't -- I'm talking about specific little examples that I might have passed on. I could have noted, yes, I found a SDS Crisis Staff in Bihac in September 1992 distributing arms, getting signatures from Serbs that they passed arms to. It's an SDS Crisis Staff that's earlier, but I don't see it as actually exculpatory. It's more a deviation from the pattern. The pattern is what I see. I'm not sure that we're understanding "exculpatory" in the same terms. "Exculpatory" are documents that, as I understand it, meet certain criteria for the -- of the Defence's position or that show somebody else was responsible for the acts. I didn't -- if I had found a consistent pattern of such documents, I would certainly have not made that part of my report and I would have brought it to the lawyers' attention. I'm not sure that I understand what you think an exculpatory document in this case would be -- I mean in the case of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will now put to you the Defence case. You were not only selective in your choice of municipalities and failed to show documents and evidence of conduct in a large number of municipalities that are a complete departure from what you describe, and you were not only selective in those documents concerning chosen municipalities but also in your choice of examples. For instance, take a look at this document that you described here. It's the issue of Foca, 18 June 1992. In paragraph 3 it says: The current civilian and military authorities of the municipality of Foca, Serb municipality of Foca -- first of all let me ask you that where there is a Serbian municipality there should also be a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any municipality where the division of the municipality was agreed upon into a Serbian and a Muslim half. The Serbs declared Serbian municipalities. They tried in some -- in a few municipalities to negotiate the borders, but they simply -- was a one-sided unilateral declaration. So I don't see that there should be a Muslim municipality of Foca. There was an elected municipal government with municipal borders established by the constitution, from which the Serbs withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, tell me, what is your answer to the suggestion Dr. Karadzic put to you that you were selective in your choice of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, my evidence is limited to that in the possession of the OTP, and documents were in many cases seized on the ground from municipalities of interest. There were municipalities which were not visited, as far as I know, by the OTP for evidence to be collected. In many places the minutes of Crisis Staffs or collections of Crisis Staff documents were not found. I could have -- I was selective in that I selected represent -- I tried to get as wide a geographical representation as I could in my selections. I could have written all of this report probably just from one or two municipalities with very good collections, but where I saw a pattern in more far -- different municipalities across Bosnia or from where we had only a small collection of evidence, I really tried to select from there just to indicate the breadth of the pattern. I did not limit myself to indictment municipalities, which then -- I heard an objection that they're not relevant. It's a balance between choosing those municipalities where some of the -- has the most attention or some of the most notorious events with showing the breadth of the pattern. I generally tried to include as broad as possible, but I know in selecting for -- certainly for annex A and B, the emphasis there was on indictment municipalities. But I was not driven by that at all in my selecting the documents for my footnotes; I was driven by the evidence available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may proceed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at this third paragraph. The first and second paragraph, first paragraph says: "The winds of war have forced many Foca inhabitants, both Serb and Muslim, to leave their houses and scatter throughout the former Yugoslavia." And then it says: "Members of families are in Foca while others are in other towns and cities." And then it goes: "The present civilian and military authorities of the Serbian municipality of Foca have so far been preventing both Serbs and Muslims from leaving the Foca territory. It is perfectly normal for every family to want to live together and it is therefore not surprising that the pressure on the civilian and military authorities is mounting every day." And then it goes in point 2: "We have learned from statements by Muslim citizens that their leadership has betrayed and abandoned them, which is an additional reason for them to leave Foca." And then it says: "While respecting the wishes of individual citizens and warning the military and civilian authorities that the lists should not include people unable to leave the territory of the Serbian municipality of Foca for security reasons, the above-named recipients are ordered to make lists complete with all the necessary information, lists of these loyal citizens who have expressed the wish to leave, who are to be informed of this decision and are give a short, signed explanation of their reasons why they want to leave the municipality." Did this find a place in your report, and why did you not find the time to cover this in the interpretation of the document you gave today?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It is clearly a War Commission deciding who can leave and organising their departure. I mention that as a theme. I don't see that that contradicts my conclusions. I don't quite understand what you're saying I should have included. It's part of -- the very fact that the War Commission is discussing this topic and is saying -- deciding who can leave and organising it I think is what's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, earlier today while representing this document and interpreting it, you made the Trial Chamber believe that Muslims were being persecuted and repressed, which this document does not show. On the contrary, it shows that the motivations of the Muslim population are met with understanding, both of the Muslims and the Serbs who wished to leave. You represented this as a sin of the Serbian authorities in Foca. Why did you not represent it properly, the way it is? It is, in fact, self-explanatory, but now the Defence has to spend much more time to show to the Trial Chamber that you misinterpreted this document, misrepresented it.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I cited this document as an example of the war commissioner being sent from the government discussing the situation in Foca, including the moving out of the population. I certainly never labelled any document a sin. That's not the way I present my evidence. As for this being the expressed wishes of the Muslims, you have to be aware of the entire situation, and I know that many of those documents that people signed saying they wished to leave were the product of stresses, pressures on them, and not a true desire to just move for the sake of it because of the war, because of the pressures on the non-Serbs, because of the situation in Foca. If I had been tasked by another investigative team to discuss pressures on Serbs in Foca and mass detaining and killing of Serbs in Foca, I might possibly have noted this document. But I simply see everywhere references to what the Serbs would -- that the Muslims wanted to leave or that their departure was organised for their own protection. And I do not find all of those credible. Part of my job in selection is choosing documents for their credibility, and the fact that Crisis Staff reports say, Out of the goodness of our heart we organise the Muslims' departure so that they would be safe somewhere else because they wanted it, it doesn't convince me. Given the other actions that they've taken, given what we know people from that area have said why they signed those things, it's disingenuous, I find. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, first of all, it says they are preventing their departure, not organising it -- I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we have to rise. There is another proceeding at 3.00 in this courtroom, so we have to move out. We'll have a somewhat long weekend and we'll resume on Tuesday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.31 p.m.,
